metaTitle: Hiring a Deck Builder in Ontario: A Homeowner's Guide
metaDescription: Wood versus composite decking, Ontario Building Code guard height rules, footing depth, permits, and timeline factors to know before hiring a deck builder.
h1: Hiring a Deck Builder in Ontario: What to Know Before You Start
summary: Material choice, guard height rules, footing depth, permits, and timeline all shape a deck project, here is what to sort out before hiring a builder.
intro: A deck is one of the more visible home projects you will take on, and also one where code requirements, material choice, and the depth of the footings matter as much as the finished look. This guide covers the decisions worth understanding before you start collecting quotes from deck builders.

sections.heading: Pressure-treated wood or composite: the real trade-offs

blocks.text: Pressure-treated wood remains the most common decking material in Ontario because it is familiar, generally less expensive up front, and easy for most builders to source and work with. It does require regular maintenance, typically cleaning and restaining every couple of years, to hold its colour and resist checking and splintering. If you are comparing the ongoing upkeep, our guide on deck and fence staining at /resources covers what that maintenance actually involves.

Composite decking, made from a blend of wood fibre and recycled plastic, generally costs more per square foot up front but requires far less annual maintenance, no staining, and tends to resist fading and splintering better over time. The trade-off is a different feel underfoot for some homeowners, and composite can run hotter in direct summer sun than lighter-coloured wood.

items: Pressure-treated wood: lower material cost, needs periodic staining or sealing, classic look, widely available
Composite: higher material cost, minimal annual maintenance, consistent colour over time, various board profiles and colours
Both materials need a structurally sound frame underneath, the frame is usually still built from pressure-treated lumber even under composite boards
Ask your builder which material they have the most recent experience installing, technique and fastener choice differ between the two

blocks.text: Get pricing for both materials in the same quote so you can compare the real difference for your specific deck size, rather than relying on general cost guidance that may not reflect your footprint or design.

sections.heading: Ontario Building Code guard and railing rules

blocks.text: Deck guards are not optional once a deck surface reaches a certain height above grade, and getting this wrong is one of the more common problems inspectors flag. Under the Ontario Building Code, a guard is generally required once the deck surface is more than about 60 centimetres, roughly 24 inches, above the ground below it.

Minimum guard heights then depend on how high the deck sits. For lower decks the minimum is commonly cited around 900 millimetres, while for decks with a greater drop, generally above about 1.8 metres, the required minimum climbs to roughly 1070 millimetres. These figures are general guidance and can vary by specific condition and municipal interpretation, so always confirm the exact requirement for your project with your municipality or your builder before finalizing a design.

items: Guard spacing between balusters is also regulated, generally to prevent a small child from passing through, confirm the exact spacing requirement locally
Stair guards and handrails have their own separate requirements distinct from the main deck guard
A builder experienced with current code should be able to explain these numbers without hesitation, if they cannot, that is worth noting

blocks.text: Guard height is not a design preference, it is a safety requirement tied to the Ontario Building Code. Confirm the exact numbers with your municipality before construction, since local interpretation and any recent updates can affect the specifics.

A deck that looks fine in its first summer can start to heave, tilt, or crack at the footings within a couple of winters if the footings were not placed below the frost line. In much of Ontario, frost depth is commonly cited around 1.2 metres, roughly 4 feet, but this varies by region and even by specific municipality, so it is not a number to guess at.

items.title: Confirm local frost depth
items.text: Ask your municipal building department for the exact frost depth requirement in your area before footing depth is finalized.

items.title: Match footing size to load
items.text: Footing diameter and depth should reflect the deck's size, height, and the soil conditions on your property, not just a standard number used everywhere.

items.title: Inspect before backfilling
items.text: Most municipalities require a footing inspection before the holes are filled, do not let a builder skip this step even if it slows the schedule.

blocks.text: Freeze-thaw cycling is the real mechanism at play here. Water in the soil around a shallow footing freezes and expands each winter, and over repeated cycles that movement can lift or shift the footing enough to throw the whole deck structure out of level. Getting the depth right the first time avoids a repair that is far more disruptive than the original build.

sections.heading: Permits: when you need one and why it matters

blocks.text: Most municipalities in Ontario require a building permit for a deck once it exceeds a certain height or size, though the exact thresholds vary from one municipality to the next. Some smaller, low platforms may be exempt, while a deck attached to the house at a meaningful height almost always needs one.

items: Check with your local building department before design work is finalized, not after
A permitted build includes inspections at key stages, footings and framing typically, which catches problems before they are buried or covered
Unpermitted decks can complicate a future home sale, since buyers and their lawyers often ask for permit records
A reputable builder will factor permit time into your project timeline rather than treating it as an afterthought

blocks.text: Ask your builder directly whether they are pulling the permit or expecting you to. This should be spelled out in the written scope of work, along with who is responsible for any fees. Our guide on /resources/contractor-red-flags covers what it means if a contractor pushes back on getting a permit at all.

sections.heading: What actually affects the build timeline

blocks.text: Deck timelines get thrown off by a handful of predictable factors, and knowing them ahead of time helps set realistic expectations with your builder.

items: Permit processing time, which can range from days to several weeks depending on your municipality's current volume
Weather, since concrete footings need proper cure time and heavy rain can delay excavation and pours
Material availability, particularly for specific composite colours or profiles that may need to be special ordered
Design complexity, multi-level decks, built-in seating, and pergola structures all add build days
Inspection scheduling, since your municipality's inspector availability is outside your builder's control

blocks.text: Get multiple quotes and ask each builder for a realistic timeline range rather than a single optimistic number. A contractor who gives you a specific, hedged answer that accounts for permits and weather is generally more trustworthy than one who promises an unrealistically fast turnaround.

checklist: Compare pressure-treated wood and composite pricing for your exact deck size
Confirm required guard height with your municipality based on deck height above grade
Confirm local frost depth before footing design is finalized
Verify whether a building permit is required for your deck's size and height
Clarify in writing who is responsible for pulling the permit
Ask about footing inspection timing before backfilling
Get a realistic timeline range that accounts for weather and permit processing
Confirm baluster spacing and stair railing requirements meet current code

faq.q: Is composite decking worth the extra upfront cost?
faq.a: It depends on how much you value low maintenance versus upfront price. Composite generally costs more per square foot but needs little annual upkeep, while pressure-treated wood costs less initially but needs periodic cleaning and staining to hold up well.

faq.q: At what height does my deck need a guard rail in Ontario?
faq.a: Guards are generally required once the deck surface is more than about 60 centimetres above grade, with minimum height requirements that increase for taller decks. Confirm the exact figures for your project with your municipality, since interpretation can vary.

faq.q: How deep do deck footings need to be in Ontario?
faq.a: Footings generally need to sit below the local frost line to avoid heaving from freeze-thaw cycling, commonly cited around 1.2 metres in much of the province, though this varies by municipality. Always confirm the exact requirement locally before construction.

faq.q: Do I need a permit for a small deck?
faq.a: It depends on your municipality's specific thresholds for height and size, some smaller platforms are exempt while decks attached to the house at a meaningful height typically require one. Check with your local building department before finalizing your design.
